      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> Vaccines</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>  (coronavirus disease 2019) is an illness caused by a <span class="qt1">virus. This virus</span> is a coronavirus called SARS-CoV-2. Most people with <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> have mild symptoms, but some people become very sick. You can protect yourself by getting a <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> vaccine. The vaccines might help keep you from getting sick from <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>. And if you do get sick, the vaccines can reduce your risk for:</p><p></p><ul><li>Needing to go to urgent care or the emergency room</li><li>Getting severe illness </li><li>Being hospitalized </li><li>Dying</li><li>Getting long COVID </li></ul><p></p><p>It's important to stay up to date with the <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> vaccines. Contact your health care provider if you don't know when you need another vaccine or if you have other questions about the vaccines.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> (coronavirus disease 2019) is a disease caused by a <span class="qt1">virus</span> called SARS-CoV-2. There are two types of tests for this <span class="qt1">virus</span>:</p><ul><li>A <span class="qt1">viral</span> test tells you if you have a current <span class="qt2">infection</span>. <span class="qt1">Viral</span> tests can either be rapid tests or laboratory tests:
 <ul><li>Rapid tests can be done in minutes. They are often antigen tests, which look for specific proteins from the <span class="qt1">virus</span>. Some rapid tests are self-tests which you can do at home.</li><li>Laboratory tests can take days to complete and include PCR tests.</li></ul>
</li><li>An antibody (serology) test might tell you if you had a past <span class="qt2">infection</span>.</li></ul><p>If you need a <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> test, you can:</p><ul><li>Buy a self-test online or at a store. Make sure that the test you buy has been authorized by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).</li><li>Check your state or local health department's website for information on testing in your area.</li><li>Contact your health care provider.</li></ul><p>Even if your <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span> <span class="qt1">viral</span> test is negative (the test did not detect the <span class="qt1">virus</span>), you should still take steps to protect yourself and others.</p><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/commoncold.html">
      <content name="title">Common Cold</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Cold, Common</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is the common cold?<p>The common cold is a mild <span class="qt2">infection</span> of your upper respiratory tract (which includes your nose and throat). Colds are probably the most common illness. Adults have an average of 2-3 colds per year, and children have even more. Colds are more common in the winter and spring, but you can get them at any time.</p>What causes the common cold?<p>More than 200 different <span class="qt1">viruses</span> can cause a cold, but rhinoviruses are the most common type. The <span class="qt1">viruses</span> that cause colds are very <span class="qt2">contagious</span>. They can spread from person to person through the air and close personal contact. You can also get infected when you touch something that has the <span class="qt1">virus</span> on it and then touch your eyes, mouth, or nose. For example, you could get a cold after you shake hands with someone who has a cold or touch a doorknob that has the germs on it, and then touch your face.</p>What are the symptoms of the common cold?<p>The symptoms of a common cold usually include:</p><ul><li>Sneezing</li><li>Stuffy nose (congestion)</li><li>Runny nose</li><li>Sore throat</li><li>Coughing</li><li>Headache</li></ul><p>The symptoms usually start a few days after you become infected with the <span class="qt1">virus</span>. Some symptoms can last for 10-14 days.</p>What are the treatments for the common cold?<p>There is no cure for the common cold. But there are treatments that can make you feel better while you wait for the cold to go away on its own:</p><ul><li>Getting lots of rest.</li><li>Drinking plenty of fluids.</li><li>Using a clean humidifier or cool mist vaporizer.</li><li>Gargling with warm salt water.</li><li>Using saline nose drops or sprays.</li><li>Taking over-the-counter pain or cold and cough medicines. But you need to be careful with certain medicines:
	<ul><li>Children and teens should not take aspirin.</li><li>Some cold and cough medicines contain ingredients that are not recommended for children. Talk with your child's health care provider before giving your child any cold and cough medicines.</li><li>Some cold and cough medicines contain pain relievers. If you also take a separate pain reliever with these medicines, you could be getting a dangerous amount of the pain reliever. Read the labels on the medicines and follow the instructions carefully. If you have questions, ask your provider or a pharmacist.</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>Antibiotics will not help with a cold. Antibiotics help with bacterial <span class="qt2">infections</span>, not with <span class="qt1">viral</span> <span class="qt2">infections</span> such as colds.</p><p>Most people who have a cold will feel better after a week or two. However, some people who get a cold may develop other illnesses, such as bronchitis or pneumonia. This is more common in people with weakened immune systems, asthma, or other respiratory conditions. Contact your provider if you or your child have symptoms that concern you, such as:</p><ul><li>Trouble breathing or fast breathing</li><li>Dehydration</li><li>Fever that lasts longer than 4 days</li><li>Symptoms that last more than 10 days without improvement</li><li>Symptoms, such as fever or cough, that improve but then return or worsen</li><li>Worsening of chronic medical conditions</li></ul>Can the common cold be prevented?<p>There is no vaccine to protect against the common cold. But you may be able to reduce your risk of getting or spreading a cold by:</p><ul><li>Washing your hands often with soap and water for at least 20 seconds.</li><li>Avoiding touching your face, nose, or mouth with unwashed hands.</li><li>Avoiding close contact, such as kissing, shaking hands, and sharing cups and eating utensils, with others if you are sick or they are sick.</li><li>Cleaning and disinfecting surfaces that you frequently touch.</li><li>Covering coughs and sneezes with a tissue. Then throw away the tissue and wash your hands.</li><li>Staying home when sick.</li></ul><p>Centers for Disease Control and Prevention</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Viral</span> <span class="qt2">Infections</span></content>

      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt2">Infections</span>, <span class="qt1">Viral</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Roseola</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are <span class="qt1">viruses</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Viruses</span> are very tiny germs. They are made of genetic material (either DNA  or RNA) inside of a protein coating. There are a huge number of <span class="qt1">viruses</span> on earth. Only a small number of them can infect humans. Those <span class="qt1">viruses</span> can infect our cells, which may cause disease. Some of the <span class="qt3">diseases that </span><span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">viruses</span></span> can cause include the common cold, the flu, <span class="qt0">COVID-19</span>, and <span class="qt1">HIV</span>.</p>How are <span class="qt1">viruses</span> spread?<p><span class="qt1">Viruses</span> can be spread in different ways:</p><ul><li>Through droplets and particles that are breathed out by someone who has the <span class="qt2">infection</span>. You might breathe in the droplets or particles, or they could land on your mouth, nose, or eyes.</li><li>By touching surfaces or objects that have the <span class="qt1">virus</span> on them and then touching your mouth, nose, or eyes.</li><li>From the pregnant parent to the baby during pregnancy.</li><li>Through contaminated food or water.</li><li>By being bitten by an infected insect or animal.</li><li>Through sexual contact (usually vaginal, anal and oral sex) with someone who has the <span class="qt2">infection</span>.</li></ul>How do <span class="qt1">viruses</span> cause disease?<p><span class="qt1">Viruses</span> are like hijackers. They invade living, normal cells. They then use those cells to multiply (make copies of themselves). This process is also called replication. The process can kill, damage, or change the infected cells. Sometimes this can make you sick. The symptoms can range from mild to very severe. Other times, your immune system may be able to fight it off and you may not have any symptoms.</p><p>Each different <span class="qt1">virus</span> usually only infects one type of cell in your body. For example, hepatitis <span class="qt1">viruses</span> affect the cells in the liver. <span class="qt1">HIV</span> infects a certain type of immune system cell. </p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">viral</span> <span class="qt2">infections</span>?<p>For most <span class="qt1">viral</span> <span class="qt2">infections</span>, treatments can only help with symptoms while you wait for your immune system to fight off the <span class="qt1">virus. There are antiviral</span> medicines to treat some <span class="qt1">viral</span> <span class="qt2">infections</span>. Antibiotics do not work for <span class="qt1">viral</span> <span class="qt2">infections</span>.</p>Can <span class="qt1">viral</span> <span class="qt2">infections</span> be prevented?<p>Vaccines can help prevent you from getting many <span class="qt1"><span class="qt3">viral</span></span><span class="qt3"> diseases</span>. You may be able to prevent some <span class="qt1">viral</span> <span class="qt2">infections</span> by:</p><ul><li>Proper hand washing.</li><li>Paying attention to food safety.</li><li>Cleaning surfaces that may be infected with germs.</li><li>Avoiding contact with wild animals.</li><li>Preventing insect bites by using insect repellent when you go outdoors. If you travel to an area that has a high risk of diseases from insect bites, also wear long pants, shirts, and socks.</li><li>Practicing safe sex (using a condom every time you have anal, vaginal, or oral sex).</li><li>Avoiding close contact with people who are sick.</li></ul></content>
